newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK Democrats sue over China-selected legislature.
newsitem.headline: HK Democrats sue over China-selected legislature.

text.p: Hong Kong's Democratic Party filed a court injunction on Tuesday to challenge the constitutional legality of Beijing's hand-picked shadow legislature set to replace a democratically-elected assembly upon the June 30 handover of the British colony.

Legal experts said the move, just 21 days before China takes over, had little chance of success but would cause intense embarrassment and may temporarily block the Beijing-selected chamber already forced to meet across the border in China.

Democratic Party legislator Albert Ho, who like fellow party members will be cast from office when the Provisional Legislature is installed, filed the writ in the High Court on behalf of party co-founder Ng King-luen, 74, the plaintiff.
"That organisation unlawfully seized law-making power which belongs solely to the present Legislative Council," Ho told reporters.
Hong Kong's democracy lobby has campaigned actively at home and overseas against the chamber, endorsed by future leader Tung Chee-hwa.
Britain and its Western allies have attacked the new assembly, questioning its legitimacy and plan to boycott any investiture ceremony.
In Washington, U.S. State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said Secretary of State Madeline Albright, who will be a guest at the handover ceremony, would not go to the swearing-in.

The Democratic Party, the most successful in Hong Kong's 1995 elections, is seeking a judicial review to proceed with its case that the 60-strong provisional chamber illegally usurped the law-making power of the elected legislature.
China, angered by mild democratic reforms introduced by last British Governor Chris Patten, has pledged to undo them.
Beijing is committed to dissolving the chamber returned in 1995 in Hong Kong's most representative election, rather than letting it serve out its four year term.

Democratic Party leader Martin Lee pledged "no surrender". He has earlier urged Britain to file an action against China over the shadow assembly at the International Court of Justice which rules on disputes between states.
He met Hong Kong's future leader Tung Chee-hwa who urged the party to refrain from proceeding but Lee said the party had no intention of backing down.
"This writ will not be cancelled ... we told him we would definitely go ahead," Lee told reporters after meeting Tung.

The provisional legislature was selected by a hand-picked panel of 400 prominent Hong Kong citizens in December and has been forced by the threat of the Democratic Party's legal action to hold its weekly meetings across the border in China.
The Democratic Party refused to cooperate with the chamber and faces at least a year in the political wilderness.
It has vowed to contest fresh elections to be staged by 1998 under new electoral rules to be devised by the Provisional Legislature.
The Democratic Party wants the courts to declare void the dozen or so bills being passed by the Provisional Legislature ahead of the handover, now just 21 days away.
Lawyers for Rita Fan, who as President of the Provisional Chamber was targeted in the writ, told the Democratic Party she would contest the case, Ho said.
Fan's spokesman declined to comment before receiving a copy of the writ. "We will decide what to do when we get the summons," he said.
